doc.title: Ken Poston interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2024

title: Success of the Mulligan Quartet at The Haig
summary: The quartet drew crowds at The Haig and sold Pacific Jazz records, but Mulligan's prison term ended the group.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Was there a financial incentive to keep the group together? Sometimes we make assumptions that these groups that find a niche and create a sound that they’re being rewarded monetarily?

I think that was — if it hadn’t already happened it was certainly coming, and it had happened to a degree because the crowds at The Haig, where they were playing, even though The Haig wasn’t very small — I mean there were literally people lined up around the block to get in. Dick Bock started the Pacific Jazz Record Company to record that group and immediately started to record them, and those records he couldn’t keep up with the demand for the records, and then immediately went up to San Francisco and played The Blackhawk and then went back to The Haig and could have certainly then gone on the road but that’s when Gerry ran into his problems and ended up in the Honor Farm for six months and that’s when the group fell apart, that particular group. So the short time that it was together it had already become a major thing within the jazz world and if it had been able, I think, to go out on the road — there really weren’t festivals yet per se in 1952-53, but there were package things happening, you know Jean Norman and Norman Granz.
So they would have certainly been in demand for those type things, but yeah it got cut short, not for musical reasons.
